questions: What happens when A_i becomes 0 after subtraction - does the index i remain usable in future moves?
Is the condition "If S=" meant to say "If S is empty" or does it refer to some other termination condition?
When the problem states "it can be proven that until a winner is determined... there exists some i such that 1≤A_i", does this guarantee apply to all possible game states or just initial states?
Does the game end immediately when S becomes empty, or only at the start of a player's turn?
What is the exact winning condition - is it when no valid moves remain, or when S is empty after a move?
Are players allowed to choose indices i where A_i = 1, knowing it might become 0 afterward?
Does the phrase "players can always make a move" mean there's always a legal move available, or that they won't get stuck in losing positions?
Is the input format strictly one line for N followed by one line for all A_i values, or could the A_i values be on multiple lines?
answers: Once an index's value is 0, it isn't usable again; a player may only choose an index while A_i ≥ 1.
'If S=' should read 'If S = {1,2,...,N}'; that's the actual termination condition, not S being empty.
The guarantee applies throughout all reachable game states until the game ends, not just the initial one.
The game ends immediately once S becomes {1,2,...,N} (not empty), right after the operation that completes it.
The winning condition is performing the operation that makes S = {1,2,...,N}; not related to S being empty.
Yes, a player may choose any index i with A_i ≥ 1, including when A_i = 1.
It means a legal move is always available until the game concludes, as explicitly guaranteed.
Not specified beyond the given two-line format; standard whitespace-separated input is assumed.
inline_prompts: Fennec and Snuke are playing a board game. You are given a positive integer N and a sequence A=(A_1,A_2,\dots,A_N) of positive integers of length N. Also, there is a set S, which is initially empty. Fennec and Snuke take turns performing the following operation in order, starting with Fennec. - Choose an index i such that A_i ≥ 1. Subtract 1 from A_i, and if i\notin S, add i to S. - If S=, the game ends and the player who performed the last operation wins. Note that it can be proven that until a winner is determined and the game ends, players can always make a move (there exists some i such that 1\leq A_i). Both Fennec and Snuke play optimally to win. Determine who will win. Input The input is given from Standard Input in the following format: N A_1 A_2 \dots A_N Output Print Fennec if Fennec wins, or Snuke if Snuke wins. The judge is case-insensitive; for example, if the correct answer is Fennec, outputs such as fennec, FENNEC, or fEnNeC will also be accepted. Constraints - 1\leq N\leq 2\times 10^5 - 1\leq A_i\leq 1^9 (1\leq i\leq N) - All input values are integers.
